title: Space Tech Briefing — September 26, 2026
summary:
Good morning, space enthusiasts, and welcome to your daily dose of cosmic currents! It's Friday, September 26, 2026, and we're kicking off the day with some truly groundbreaking developments from the final frontier. Get ready to launch into the latest!

First up, as we reflect on some major recent developments, let's talk about a shining example of international collaboration and French expertise. The far-infrared camera, PRIMAger, has been officially selected by NASA! This incredible instrument will be one of the two key components of the upcoming PRIMA mission. We're hearing from experts at CNES, the French space agency, who are highlighting this significant French contribution to international science. It's a testament to the cutting-edge capabilities being developed right here on Earth to explore the universe in new ways.

And speaking of incredible discoveries, let's cast our gaze towards our celestial neighbor, the Moon! Scientists have recently unveiled what's being called the largest impact crater discovered in a century. This massive scar on the lunar surface was found using high-resolution images from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, or LRO. The crater itself measures a staggering 222 meters in diameter, and it's surrounded by an even larger "cold spot" spanning a remarkable 7 kilometers wide. This colossal impact event occurred between April 11th and May 22nd of 2024, when an asteroid or comet, estimated to be the size of a three to six-story building, slammed into the lunar surface. The crater is approximately 43 meters deep and has been officially named in honor of the late American scientist Tom McGetchin, a renowned geologist and planetologist who specialized in impact craters. What a find, giving us fresh insights into the Moon's dynamic history!

And that's your space technology briefing for this September 26th, 2026. Thank you for joining us on this journey through the cosmos. Stay curious, keep looking up, and we'll catch you next time for more out-of-this-world news!
